hook_text: A stool covered in gold that no one, not even the king, was allowed to sit on. It held a nation together for two hundred years.
clip_script: Around 1700, in the forests of what is now Ghana, Osei Tutu united the Asante chiefdoms. His priest, Okomfo Anokye, brought forth the Golden Stool, holding the spirit of the whole nation. The chiefs buried their own stools. Osei Tutu became Asantehene. Kumasi became a planned capital with great roads running out to the whole empire. Gold dust was money. Kola nuts went north. On the coast, Europeans had built forts since 1482, but they paid rent to African rulers and never ruled the interior. In 1817, a British envoy walked into Kumasi and was astonished. In 1824, the Asante defeated a British army. This was a power to be reckoned with.
visual_style: A whiteboard Golden Stool at centre, roads radiating from Kumasi on a map, a coastline lined with fort icons, and a timeline from 1482 to 1824.
pacing: Story-like opening, brisk middle, strong close.
